碳矽之間 About this site

人類歷史上的每一次技術革命，都曾改變我們理解世界的方式。

攝影、電影、電腦與網際網路的誕生，新的媒介不斷擴展人類感知、記錄與創造世界的能力。每一次變革都伴隨焦慮與質疑，但也同時重新定義了文明的樣貌。

今日，人工智慧正成為下一個改變世界的重要力量。

然而，人工智慧所帶來的衝擊並不僅止於技術層面。當它開始參與影像生成、文字創作、音樂製作與文化生產，人類首次如此直接地面對一個問題：如果創作不再是人類獨有的能力，我們應該如何重新理解創造本身？

過去數百年間，人類始終是文化與藝術的主要生產者。我們以繪畫描繪世界，以攝影保存真實，以文字建構思想，以藝術回應時代。創作不只是技術的展現，更是情感、經驗與價值觀的累積。

然而生成式人工智慧的出現，正在改變這項長久以來的前提。

當一段文字即可生成圖像，當演算法能夠模仿風格、重組文化符號、創造從未存在過的畫面，創作者與工具之間的界線開始變得模糊。作者是誰？創作權屬於誰？藝術的價值究竟來自作品本身，還是來自創作背後的意圖與經驗？

2026年被稱為Physical AI元年

《碳矽之間》希望透過藝術作品、生成影像與公共討論，建立一個重新思考創作本質的場域。

本展以「碳基生命」與「矽基智慧」作為象徵。碳，代表人類的情感、記憶與生命經驗；矽，代表運算、演算法與新興智慧系統。兩者並非對立，而是在當代文化之中逐漸形成新的共生關係。

因此，本展關注的從來不是人工智慧是否會取代人類，而是當新的智慧形式開始與人類共同創造世界時，我們將如何重新定義自身的位置。

Every technological revolution in human history has fundamentally reshaped how we perceive and conceptualize the world.

With the advent of photography, cinema, computing, and the internet, new media have continuously expanded humanity’s capacity to perceive, record, and construct reality. While each profound shift has been accompanied by anxiety and skepticism, it has invariably redefined the very contours of civilization.

Today, artificial intelligence is emerging as the next monumental force transforming our world.

However, the impact of AI extends far beyond the realm of pure technology. As it actively participates in image generation, textual composition, musical production, and cultural creation, humanity is confronted—for the very first time—with a profound question: If creation is no longer an exclusively human domain, how must we re-evaluate and understand the act of creation itself?

For centuries, humans have been the primary authors of culture and art. We have depicted the world through painting, preserved reality through photography, constructed thought through literature, and responded to our respective eras through art. Creation is never merely a demonstration of technical skill; it is the culmination of emotion, lived experience, and values.

Yet, the rise of generative AI is dismantling this long-held premise.

When a single string of text can instantly generate an image, and when algorithms can mimic styles, reconfigure cultural symbols, and conjure visuals that have never previously existed, the boundaries between the creator and the tool begin to blur. Who is the author? To whom does authorship belong? Does the value of art reside within the artifact itself, or does it stem from the intent and experience behind its creation?

2026 is heralded as the inaugural year of Physical AI.

Through contemporary artworks, generative imagery, and public discourse, "Between Carbon and Silicon" seeks to cultivate a discursive space for rethinking the essence of creation.

This exhibition adopts "carbon-based life" and "silicon-based intelligence" as its central metaphors. Carbon represents human emotion, memory, and existential experience; silicon signifies computation, algorithms, and emerging intelligent systems. Rather than viewing them as binary opposites, this exhibition explores how the two are gradually forming a new symbiotic relationship within contemporary culture.

Ultimately, the focus of this exhibition is not whether artificial intelligence will replace humanity, but rather how we will redefine our own position when new forms of intelligence begin to co-create the world alongside us.

碳矽之間 緣起

人類歷史上的每一次技術革命，都曾改變我們理解世界的方式。

攝影、電影、電腦與網際網路的誕生，新的媒介不斷擴展人類感知、記錄與創造世界的能力。每一次變革都伴隨焦慮與質疑，但也同時重新定義了文明的樣貌。

今日，人工智慧正成為下一個改變世界的重要力量。

然而，人工智慧所帶來的衝擊並不僅止於技術層面。當它開始參與影像生成、文字創作、音樂製作與文化生產，人類首次如此直接地面對一個問題：如果創作不再是人類獨有的能力，我們應該如何重新理解創造本身？

過去數百年間，人類始終是文化與藝術的主要生產者。我們以繪畫描繪世界，以攝影保存真實，以文字建構思想，以藝術回應時代。創作不只是技術的展現，更是情感、經驗與價值觀的累積。

然而生成式人工智慧的出現，正在改變這項長久以來的前提。

當一段文字即可生成圖像，當演算法能夠模仿風格、重組文化符號、創造從未存在過的畫面，創作者與工具之間的界線開始變得模糊。作者是誰？創作權屬於誰？藝術的價值究竟來自作品本身，還是來自創作背後的意圖與經驗？

2026年被稱為Physical AI元年

《碳矽之間》希望透過藝術作品、生成影像與公共討論，建立一個重新思考創作本質的場域。

本展以「碳基生命」與「矽基智慧」作為象徵。碳，代表人類的情感、記憶與生命經驗；矽，代表運算、演算法與新興智慧系統。兩者並非對立，而是在當代文化之中逐漸形成新的共生關係。

因此，本展關注的從來不是人工智慧是否會取代人類，而是當新的智慧形式開始與人類共同創造世界時，我們將如何重新定義自身的位置。

Every technological revolution in human history has fundamentally reshaped how we perceive and conceptualize the world.

With the advent of photography, cinema, computing, and the internet, new media have continuously expanded humanity’s capacity to perceive, record, and construct reality. While each profound shift has been accompanied by anxiety and skepticism, it has invariably redefined the very contours of civilization.

Today, artificial intelligence is emerging as the next monumental force transforming our world.

However, the impact of AI extends far beyond the realm of pure technology. As it actively participates in image generation, textual composition, musical production, and cultural creation, humanity is confronted—for the very first time—with a profound question: If creation is no longer an exclusively human domain, how must we re-evaluate and understand the act of creation itself?

For centuries, humans have been the primary authors of culture and art. We have depicted the world through painting, preserved reality through photography, constructed thought through literature, and responded to our respective eras through art. Creation is never merely a demonstration of technical skill; it is the culmination of emotion, lived experience, and values.

Yet, the rise of generative AI is dismantling this long-held premise.

When a single string of text can instantly generate an image, and when algorithms can mimic styles, reconfigure cultural symbols, and conjure visuals that have never previously existed, the boundaries between the creator and the tool begin to blur. Who is the author? To whom does authorship belong? Does the value of art reside within the artifact itself, or does it stem from the intent and experience behind its creation?

2026 is heralded as the inaugural year of Physical AI.

Through contemporary artworks, generative imagery, and public discourse, "Between Carbon and Silicon" seeks to cultivate a discursive space for rethinking the essence of creation.

This exhibition adopts "carbon-based life" and "silicon-based intelligence" as its central metaphors. Carbon represents human emotion, memory, and existential experience; silicon signifies computation, algorithms, and emerging intelligent systems. Rather than viewing them as binary opposites, this exhibition explores how the two are gradually forming a new symbiotic relationship within contemporary culture.

Ultimately, the focus of this exhibition is not whether artificial intelligence will replace humanity, but rather how we will redefine our own position when new forms of intelligence begin to co-create the world alongside us.

From Dehua Blanc de Chine and Zhangzhou wares produced in seventeenth and eighteenth century Fujian to the silicon wafers that power artificial intelligence today, silicon has never been merely a technological material; it has also served as one of civilisation’s most important material carriers. Quartz, feldspar, and Kaolin are transformed by fire into ceramics, just as crystalline silicon is processed through highly precise fabrication into semiconductor chips. Both
originate from closely related mineral foundations, yet embody the knowledge and ingenuity of different periods in human history.

Displayed alongside the large Zhangzhou underglaze blue dish are Dehua wares, a ceramic tradition that profoundly influenced European porcelain.
Dehua is located in present-day Dehua County, Quanzhou, Fujian, China. Although its mountainous landscape was not well suited to agriculture, its
ranges of hills, extensive waterways, and distinctive mineral-rich soils provided
the essential resources for ceramic production. Dehua porcelain is characterised by high-temperature firing, a closely integrated body and glaze, and a refined, luminous white appearance. In contrast to the comparatively coarse bodies of Zhangzhou export wares, its whiteness reflects the low concentration of iron and other colouring impurities in the raw materials.

Dehua potters produced an unusually broad range of forms, including vessels, scholar’s objects, devotional figures, and sculptures—less commonly found together at other kilns.

Dehua was also an important export ceramic. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, large quantities reached Europe aboard international trading vessels. French collectors came to call it Blanc de Chine, or “Chinese
white.” The designation continues to evoke the distinctive ivory white associated with Dehua porcelain; nowadays, Pantone colour 11-4800 likewise bears the name Blanc de Chine.

Dehua porcelain was exported to maritime powers such as Portugal, Spain, and
the Netherlands, while Britain also developed a strong interest in these wares. From the late seventeenth to the early eighteenth century, the British East India Company transported substantial quantities of Dehua porcelain to Britain. The Dehua chocolate cup and saucer applied with prunus branches here are derived from European vessel forms and can be compared with an example
in the collection of the British Museum.

Important European collections of Dehua porcelain were assembled at royal sites including Blenheim Palace in England and the Zwinger Palace in Dresden, now in eastern Germany. Augustus II the Strong, Elector of Saxony from 1694 to 1733, was an especially enthusiastic collector of Dehua porcelain and other East
Asian ceramics. His collection directly contributed to the development of European porcelain production. Numerous works produced by Meissen,
celebrated as Germany’s “white gold,” as well as by Bow Porcelain in England, reveal the influence of Dehua wares and its white porcelain aesthetics.

The small drum-shaped covered box positioned at the front may appear at first glance to be Dehua blanc de Chine. It is, however, a Southern Song dynasty Jingdezhen Qingbai porcelain box dated 12/13th century. Its subtly blue-tinged
glaze differs from the warmer ivory-white tones of Dehua porcelain. Visitors are
invited to observe and appreciate the delicate distinction between the two.

Inspired by map art and the urban fabric of Taichung, this work transforms the city's street network into an intricate composition of colored pencil strokes. At its center, the circular form of Taichung's Ring Road (Huanzhong Road) emerges as the city's defining structure, from which the surrounding streets unfold like an organic network. Layer upon layer of delicate lines resemble the traces of time, while simultaneously evoking the countless paths created by generations of citizens, revealing Taichung's unique cultural landscape and collective memory.

The pair of hands hovering above the city symbolizes protection, cultivation, and guidance. They suggest that shaping a city is much like creating a work of art—an enduring process that demands patience, vision, and unwavering commitment. A city's true identity is not defined solely by its buildings or roads, but by its culture, education, industries, and, above all, the people whose lives continually shape its character.

By transforming a map into a work of art, the painting invites viewers to see the city itself as an ever-evolving masterpiece. It celebrates Taichung as a place where tradition and innovation converge, expressing the enduring vitality of a city that continues to grow, inspire, and create its future.

在臺灣的集體記憶中，媽祖不只是航海者的守護神，更是一種跨越世代的母性象徵。她承載的不只是宗教信仰，更是人們對平安、包容與歸屬的共同寄託。她既是信仰的守護者，也是無數生命故事的陪伴者；在人們一次次出海、返鄉、遷徙與生活之中，共同參與了這片土地文化與文明的創造。

本作品以東方膠彩畫為主要媒材語彙，透過細膩而溫潤的色層，重新詮釋東方女性的典雅之美。畫面沒有刻意強調神性的威嚴，而是以低垂的眼神、柔和的輪廓與安靜的姿態，呈現一位母親凝視生命時的慈悲與溫暖。她不僅是信仰的象徵，更是一位孕育希望、陪伴創作者與每一位追尋者前行的精神原型。

創作靈感融合文藝復興藝術中三種不同的母性精神：汲取李奧納多·達文西對自然與生命和諧共生的哲學，使人物與雲霧、天地融為一體；借鑑巴托洛梅·埃斯特萬·穆里羅筆下聖母溫柔而包容的情感氛圍；並參考拉斐爾平衡、莊嚴而優雅的構圖，建立人物沉靜而永恆的精神性。同時，作品以東方膠彩的層層積染，重新轉譯西方藝術史中的母性精神，讓不同文明的美學在同一畫面中彼此對話、共同創作。

Voyage of Compassion

Within Taiwan's collective memory, Mazu is far more than the guardian deity of seafarers. She embodies a timeless symbol of motherhood, transcending generations and religious traditions alike. Beyond faith, she represents humanity's shared longing for peace, compassion, and belonging. As both a protector of belief and a silent companion to countless lives, Mazu has accompanied people through voyages across the sea, journeys home, migration, and everyday life—becoming a co-creator of the cultural identity and civilization of this land.

Rendered in the visual language of traditional East Asian nihonga-inspired mineral pigments, this work reinterprets the elegance and quiet strength of Eastern femininity through delicate layers of luminous color. Rather than emphasizing divine authority, the composition presents Mazu with a lowered gaze, gentle contours, and serene poise, revealing the warmth and compassion of a mother contemplating life itself. She is not merely an icon of faith, but an enduring archetype who nurtures hope and accompanies creators, dreamers, and seekers on their journeys.

The work draws inspiration from three distinct visions of motherhood in Renaissance art. It embraces Leonardo da Vinci's philosophy of harmony between humanity and nature, allowing the figure to dissolve seamlessly into clouds, sky, and earth. It echoes the tender compassion found in Bartolomé Esteban Murillo's Madonnas, while adopting Raphael's balanced compositions and graceful serenity to evoke a timeless spiritual presence. Through the layered techniques of Eastern mineral painting, the work reinterprets the maternal ideals of Western art history, creating a dialogue in which Eastern and Western aesthetics meet, coexist, and become co-creators within a single image.

The drifting clouds symbolize sea mist and the perpetual movement between heaven and earth. Her richly adorned robe, woven with dragon motifs and traditional decorative patterns, alludes to maritime culture, collective memory, and the enduring legacy of Eastern craftsmanship. In this painting, Mazu is not only the Heavenly Holy Mother of faith, but also a universal mother who accompanies generations of creators, safeguards cultural heritage, and guides humanity safely through the uncertainties of life.

She protects not only those who journey across the sea, but also the enduring values of compassion, courage, hope, and the civilization we continue to create together.

當人工智慧逐漸能夠生成近乎完美的形象，人類真正無可取代的價值，不再只是設計一件衣服，而是理解每一個生命的獨特性，並以美學喚醒自信、尊嚴與個人風格。

一件衣裳，可以改變一個人的氣質；一種品味，可以定義一個時代。

作品以優雅的人物輪廓象徵人性的美，白色厚塗油彩如同被歲月反覆雕琢的高級訂製布料，既保留手工創作的溫度，也呈現藝術與時尚交融的生命力。畫面沒有追求華麗的裝飾，而是透過細膩的肌理與沉靜的姿態，描繪真正的美並非來自外表，而是來自眼光、文化與時間的積累。

當人工智慧逐漸能夠生成近乎完美的形象，人類真正無可取代的價值，不再只是設計一件衣服，而是理解每一個生命的獨特性，並以美學喚醒自信、尊嚴與個人風格。

科技可以複製形式，卻無法複製品味；演算法可以學習風格，卻無法承襲一位創作者數十年淬鍊而成的審美與匠心。真正的時尚，從來不是流行，而是文明對美的持續追求。這正是《碳矽之間》希望探討的人本價值：當科技愈發強大，真正值得被傳承的，仍是人類創造美、理解美，並以美影響世界的能力。

本作品承襲 Alphonse Mucha 所代表的新藝術運動（Art Nouveau）對自然、曲線與裝飾美學的探索，同時融合當代 Fashion Fine Art 的時尚影像語言，使人體藝術、服裝設計與繪畫媒材跨越不同創作領域，在 AI 時代重新思考「美」的本質與人的不可取代性。

A single garment can transform an individual's presence; refined taste can define an entire era.

This work portrays the elegance of human nature through the graceful silhouette of a figure. Layers of richly textured white impasto evoke the drape of haute couture, embodying both the warmth of handcrafted artistry and the vitality found at the intersection of art and fashion. Rather than relying on ornate decoration, the composition embraces subtle textures and quiet poise to suggest that true beauty is not merely an outward appearance, but the result of cultivated vision, cultural depth, and the passage of time.

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly capable of generating images of near-perfect beauty, humanity's irreplaceable value lies no longer simply in designing garments, but in recognizing the uniqueness of every individual and using aesthetics to awaken confidence, dignity, and personal identity.

Technology can replicate form, but it cannot replicate taste. Algorithms may learn styles, yet they cannot inherit the refined aesthetic judgment and craftsmanship shaped through decades of creative practice. True fashion has never been about following trends; it is an enduring pursuit of beauty that reflects the evolution of civilization. This is the human-centered value explored in Between Carbon and Silicon: as technology grows ever more powerful, what remains truly worth preserving is humanity's ability to create beauty, understand beauty, and shape the world through it.

Drawing inspiration from the Art Nouveau movement, as embodied by Alphonse Mucha, this work explores the expressive language of nature, flowing lines, and ornamental elegance while incorporating the visual vocabulary of contemporary Fashion Fine Art. By bringing together figurative art, fashion design, and painterly expression, it invites viewers to reconsider the nature of beauty and the irreplaceable role of human creativity in the age of artificial intelligence.

本作品汲取 American Regionalism 對土地、人群與真實生活的關注，融合 Contemporary Fine Art 的空間語彙，以一面巨大的鏡面作為畫面的核心，探討科技、媒體與人文價值之間的關係。

在《碳矽之間》的語境中，這件作品提出了一個簡單卻重要的命題：未來值得被照見的，不只是更先進的科技，而是始終以人文為本的文明。

Drawing on American Regionalism and its attention to land, community, and everyday life, this work incorporates the spatial language of Contemporary Fine Art. A monumental mirror occupies the center of the composition, serving as a visual and conceptual device through which the relationships among technology, media, and humanistic values are examined.

The reflection within the mirror does not reveal another world; it reflects the civilization we collectively inhabit. Distant mountains, light shimmering across the lake, and the meeting of earth and sky symbolize the enduring order of nature and timeless values. Beyond the mirror, geometrically constructed cities, buildings, and human figures evoke a modern world shaped by technological development, the circulation of information, and social transformation. A solitary figure stands before the mirror, both observer and observed, inviting us to reconsider a fundamental question: as technology becomes ever more powerful, should we be looking toward the future—or more closely at ourselves?

The mission of journalism is to reflect society faithfully; the responsibility of corporate governance is to uphold principles amid change. The mirror therefore becomes more than a surface that reflects light. It symbolizes integrity, judgment, and public trust. It reminds us that technology may accelerate the flow of information, but it cannot determine the direction of our values. The future is ultimately shaped by how human beings understand truth, assume responsibility, and make choices.

Within the context of Between Carbon and Silicon, this work presents a simple yet essential proposition: what deserves to be reflected in the future is not only more advanced technology, but a civilization that remains firmly grounded in humanistic values.

枯山水並非直接描繪山川河流，而是透過砂紋、石塊與留白，引導觀者在有限之中感受無限，在靜止之中體會時間的流動。這種「以少見多」的東方哲學，也映照真正的工藝精神——不是追求表面的繁複，而是在每一道工序中不斷修正、精進與淬鍊，直至成就歷久彌新的品質。

這份精神亦與茶藝相通。從選水、候湯、置茶、注水到奉茶，每一個動作看似簡約，實則來自長時間的練習與對當下的專注。茶席所重視的，不只是技法，更是「一期一會」的心意：每一次相遇、每一席茶、每一位來客，都只存在於當下，無法複製，也不會重來。正因如此，職人更以敬意對待每一個細節，使短暫的一刻成為值得珍藏的記憶。

作品中的層層紋理，隱含木作工藝、手工雕琢與茶席行止所形成的節奏，如同職人反覆打磨器物、整理庭院、溫壺候茶，將平凡的材料與日常動作轉化為具有精神性的創作。每一道耙紋都不是偶然，而是耐心、經驗與時間共同留下的印記；真正的價值，往往誕生於那些最容易被忽略的細節之中。

畫面中央靜置的岩石象徵初心與本質。無論時代如何變遷，真正能夠歷久彌新的，不是形式，而是始終如一的匠心。每一件經典作品、每一項精湛工藝、每一次真誠的奉茶，皆來自日復一日的累積，而非一蹴可幾的完成。

當智慧科技逐漸改變世界，真正值得珍惜的，仍是人所擁有的專注、耐心與對品質近乎執著的追求。科技可以提升效率，卻無法取代職人對細節的感知，也無法複製一期一會的真實相遇。真正能跨越世代流傳的，不只是作品與技藝本身，而是那份以一生反覆琢磨、以真心對待每一次相遇的職人精神。

Inspired by the contemplative aesthetics of the Japanese Karesansui (dry landscape garden), this work explores the dialogue between time, nature, and craftsmanship through a language of refined simplicity. The flowing patterns in the raked sand are not accidental traces of nature, but the result of deliberate, repeated gestures. Every line reflects a craftsman's unwavering pursuit of order, beauty, and precision.

Rather than depicting mountains and rivers literally, the dry landscape garden evokes the vastness of nature through carefully composed gravel, stone, and empty space. Within what appears minimal lies an infinite landscape for contemplation. This philosophy of "expressing the infinite through the essential" mirrors the true spirit of craftsmanship—not the pursuit of complexity, but the continual refinement of every detail until timeless quality emerges.

This philosophy is equally embodied in the Japanese tea ceremony. From selecting the water and preparing the tea to each measured movement of serving, every gesture is simple in appearance yet rooted in years of discipline and mindful practice. At the heart of the tea ceremony is the principle of Ichigo Ichie—"one time, one meeting"—the understanding that every encounter is unique and can never be repeated. It is this awareness that inspires artisans to devote themselves wholeheartedly to every moment, transforming an ordinary encounter into an unforgettable experience.

The layered textures within the composition subtly evoke woodworking, handcraftsmanship, and the quiet rhythm of preparing tea. Like a craftsman patiently refining a piece of wood, tending a Zen garden, or performing a tea ceremony, each carefully drawn line becomes a testament to patience, experience, and the passage of time. True excellence is often found not in what immediately captures attention, but in the countless details that quietly shape the whole.

At the center of the composition rests a solitary stone, symbolizing origin, integrity, and unwavering purpose. While times continue to change, what endures is not outward form but the spirit of craftsmanship itself. Every timeless work, every masterful craft, and every sincere bowl of tea is born through years of dedication rather than instant achievement.

As intelligent technologies continue to reshape our world, the qualities that remain uniquely human are focus, patience, and an uncompromising commitment to excellence. Technology may enhance efficiency, but it cannot replace the artisan's sensitivity to detail, nor can it recreate the authenticity of Ichigo Ichie—the irreplaceable value of a single shared moment. What ultimately transcends generations is not merely the object that is created, but the enduring spirit of craftsmanship and the sincerity with which each encounter is embraced.

This work brings together the geometric order of De Stijl, the structural principles of Rationalism, and the minimalist language of Contemporary Architectural Fine Art. Through a sequence of receding architectural spaces, it explores the enduring relationship between freedom, trust, and civilization.

A series of doorways extends toward the horizon, functioning simultaneously as architectural forms and as a timeline of human progress. Each threshold represents an era, an institution, and a choice. Though connected in sequence, every doorway remains open, preserving the possibility of moving forward into new spaces. True freedom is not the absence of order, but the ability for ideas to advance within a stable and enduring framework.

Although no human figures appear in the composition, human presence is felt throughout. Space becomes a metaphor for civilization, while architecture symbolizes the structures of trust upon which society is built. As technology rapidly reshapes the world, what humanity must preserve is not merely the pace of innovation, but the shared values of freedom, responsibility, and public trust that give progress its meaning.

The composition's balance, proportion, and geometric rhythm echo the De Stijl movement's pursuit of universal order while reflecting contemporary aspirations for sound governance and institutional integrity. The light that emerges at the end of the architectural passage is not an endpoint, but a symbol of hope and continuity—a reminder that civilization advances through reason, thoughtful inquiry, and the trust we build together.

卡片梭織簡介: Introduction to Tablet Weaving


這裡展示的所有織帶都不是織布機織造的，而是運用一種古老的紡織技法——如今被稱為「卡片梭織」織作而成。卡片梭織曾廣泛流傳於世界許多早期文明，包括北非、中亞、歐洲、冰島以及亞洲部分地區。儘管人們常常誤以為卡片梭織是織布機織造的前身，但兩者在技術原理和結構體系上都存在根本性的差異。

卡片梭織發展成為一種獨立的紡織傳統，擁有其獨特的工藝、歷史和文化意義。
縱觀歷史，卡片織帶的用途十分廣泛。在古代社會，人們用它們製作牲畜的皮帶、挽具和拴繩。到了中世紀，它們演變為精美絕倫的裝飾飾帶，點綴著歐洲貴族和神職人員的華貴服飾。如今，當代纖維藝術家們仍在運用這項技法，透過創新的紡織藝術探索其豐富的創作潛力。
從中世紀到文藝復興時期，織帶工藝在歐洲蓬勃發展，達到了技藝和藝術造詣的巔峰。然而，隨著工業革命的到來，這項工藝逐漸衰落，並在接下來的幾個世紀中幾乎被遺忘。直到19世紀末，德國學者瑪格麗特·萊曼-菲爾赫斯發表了她開創性的研究，重新喚起了人們對織帶工藝的興趣。她的研究證明，考古學家發掘出的穿孔的卡片其實就是用來編織這些古代織帶的工具。她的工作為織帶工藝的現代復興奠定了基礎。織帶片的形狀多種多樣，包括正方形、長方形、三角形和六邊形，每種形狀都提供了獨特的結構可能性和圖案編織方法。這次展出的五件作品多由四十片正方形卡片編織而成，每片織帶片上都鑽有四個孔。考古發現的卡片由木頭、角、骨頭和皮革製成。現代織造者通常使用厚紙板、壓克力板或竹板。經線穿過一系列織片的孔洞並繃緊後，織卡片前後翻轉，同時穿入緯線。透過控制織片的旋轉，可以織出種類繁多的幾何圖案、紋理和編織結構。

卡片梭織的真正精妙之處在於，它只用最簡單的工具就能織出複雜精巧的設計。即使在今天，卡片梭織片的織帶也沒有採用機器進行商業化生產。每一條織帶都完全由手工編織而成，保留了手工紡織品獨有的微妙紋理、豐富的觸感和溫暖的質感。


None of the woven bands presented here were produced on a loom. Instead, they were created usingan ancient textile technique known today as tablet weaving (also called card weaving).
Tablet weaving was practiced across many of the world's early civilizations, including North Africa,Central Asia, Europe, Iceland, and parts of Asia. Although often mistaken for a precursor to loomweaving, the two are fundamentally different in both their technical principles and structural systems.
Tablet weaving developed as an independent textile tradition with its own methods, history, and cultural significance.
Throughout history, tablet-woven bands have served a remarkable range of purposes. In ancient societies, they were used to make straps, harnesses, and tethers for livestock. By the Middle Ages, they had evolved into exquisitely woven decorative trims that embellished the luxurious garments of European nobility and the clergy. Today, contemporary fiber artists continue to embrace the technique,
exploring its rich creative potential through innovative textile art.
Tablet weaving flourished in Europe from the medieval period through the Renaissance, reaching an exceptional level of technical and artistic refinement. With the advent of the Industrial Revolution, however, the craft gradually declined and remained largely forgotten for several centuries. Interest was rekindled in the late nineteenth century when the German scholar Margarethe Lehmann-Filhés
published her groundbreaking research, demonstrating that the perforated tablets unearthed by archaeologists were, in fact, the tools used for weaving these ancient bands. Her work laid the foundation for the modern revival of tablet weaving.
Weaving tablets have been made in a variety of shapes—including square, rectangular, triangular, and hexagonal forms—each offering distinct structural possibilities and patterning methods. Most of the five works exhibited here were woven using forty square tablets, each pierced with four holes.
Archaeological examples of weaving tablets have been found fashioned from wood, horn, bone, and leather. Modern practitioners commonly use heavy card, acrylic, or bamboo. After the warp threads are passed through the holes of a series of tablets and placed under tension, the tablets are turned forward and backward while the weft thread is inserted. Through the controlled rotation of the tablets,
an extraordinary range of geometric patterns, textures, and woven structures can be achieved.
What makes tablet weaving truly remarkable is its ability to produce intricate and sophisticated designs with only the simplest of tools. Even today, tablet-woven bands have not been commercialized through machine production. Every band is woven entirely by hand, preserving the subtle irregularities, rich texture, and warmth that are unique to handcrafted textiles.

福建崎嶇的地形和有限的耕地使海上貿易對當地生存至關重要。明初的海禁導致了廣泛的走私甚至海盜，漳州月港逐漸成為主要的貿易港口。從15世紀中葉開始，月港在出口中國瓷器方面發揮了至關重要的作用；16世紀末歐洲商人的到來進一步擴大了貿易。1567年明政府正式將月港指定為合法的外貿港口，以減少腐敗，增加收入，並加強抵禦日本海盜。 這一決定鞏固了月港在明朝晚期作為國際貿易中心的地位。漳州豐富的陶瓷資源及靠近月港，再加上日本和東南亞諸國的貿易需求及歐洲人的商業野心的相互作用下，大力推動了漳州窯業的增長。

在營銷和定價策略上漳州窯遵循了宋元時期南方民窯的模式，針對海外低端市場大量生產傾銷。故在東南亞、日本、非洲和美洲的古代遺址、沉船和考古遺蹟中都有發現了大量漳州器。

明朝滅亡後，漳州的陶瓷產業也開始衰落。當國姓爺鄭成功將荷蘭人驅逐出臺灣時，福建沿海和廣東成為晚明抗清勢力的前線，清政府加強沿海撤離更加劇了漳州的衰落。海禁雖在1682年康熙年間解除，但月港的貿易作用已經被廈門接管，最終，漳州窯的生產被泉州的德化和周邊地區的窯業所取代。

漳州窯的研究可以為晚明海商世界的經濟、技術和文化交流提供了寶貴的見解。這些漳州器以其自由無拘束的裝飾風格、豪邁的尺寸，和獨特的沙礫而聞名，主要在漳州平和縣生產，並大量出口到東南亞、日本、中東、歐洲、甚至美洲。本件漳州釉下青花帆船羅盤大皿原為葡萄牙私人收藏家所有，現為臺灣沐錦堂收藏，類似的大盤也可見於日本大阪東洋陶磁館、東京出光美術館、東京靜嘉堂等。

Ceramics are among the oldest media that exist between carbon and silicon. Their creation depends on silica-rich minerals such as quartz, feldspar, and
kaolin, transformed by carbon-fuelled fire and shaped by the skilled hands and imagination of human beings. Ceramics are therefore one of humanity's earliest material manifestations of the collaboration between carbon and silicon.

The late Ming Swatow (Zhangzhou) underglaze blue dish and Qing dynasty
Dehua Blanc de Chine wares presented in Past Is a Foreign Land form the conceptual core of this exhibition. Between Carbon and Silicon is not simply an exhibition about artificial intelligence or semiconductors; rather, it returns to a more fundamental proposition—that human civilisation has always been built upon the continuous collaboration between carbon and silicon. Long before
silicon wafers became the foundation of contemporary computing, people had
already transformed silica-bearing minerals into ceramics through fire, producing objects that carried memory, belief, trade, and culture across
generations.

The large underglaze blue Swatow dish with compass and sailing boat decoration exhibited here was formerly in a private Portuguese collection. It represents not only maritime trade and global circulation during the late Ming dynasty, but also Fujian homeland from which many Han settlers later migrated to Taiwan.

Fujian's mountainous terrain and limited agricultural land made overseas trade essential to regional survival. During the Ming dynasty, restrictions on maritime trade encouraged widespread smuggling and piracy, while Yuegang (Moon
Harbour) in Zhangzhou gradually emerged as one of China's most important
international ports. From the mid-fifteenth century onwards, Yuegang became a major centre for the export of Chinese ceramics. The arrival of European merchants during the late sixteenth century further expanded global trade, and
in 1567 the Ming government officially opened Yuegang as a legal foreign trading port, strengthening its position as one of East Asia's principal maritime hubs.

Supported by abundant ceramic resources, proximity to Yuegang, growing demand from Japan and Southeast Asia, and expanding European commercial
networks, the Zhangzhou kilns flourished as one of the largest export ceramic industries of the late Ming period. Following the production model established by
provincial kilns during the Song and Yuan dynasties, Zhangzhou potters specialised in large-scale production for overseas markets. As a result, Zhangzhou wares have been recovered from archaeological sites, shipwrecks,
and historical settlements throughout Southeast Asia, Japan, the Middle East, Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

Following the fall of the Ming dynasty in 1644, Zhangzhou's ceramic industry gradually declined. The coastal wars surrounding Koxinga’s resistance against the Qing dynasty, together with the Qing coastal evacuation policy, severely disrupted maritime production and trade. Although the maritime ban was lifted
in 1682 during the Kangxi reign, Yuegang had already been replaced by Xiamen as the region's principal trading port, and Zhangzhou's ceramic production was gradually superseded by the kilns of Dehua and neighbouring Quanzhou.

Today, Zhangzhou ceramics continue to provide invaluable insights into the economy, technology, and cultural exchanges of the late Ming maritime world.

Renowned for their monumental scale, spontaneous brushwork, and distinctive sandy kiln grit, these export wares remain among the most recognisable
products of early globalisation. The present dish, formerly in a private Portuguese collection and now courtesy of the Mujintang Collection, is
comparable to examples preserved in the Osaka Municipal Museum of Art, the
Idemitsu Museum of Arts in Tokyo, and the Seikado Bunko Art Museum.

陶瓷是碳與矽之間最古老的媒介—以炭火作為燃料、由石英、長石、高嶺土等富含矽元素的礦物高溫燒製而成，最後透過陶工的巧思捏塑出作品，承載跨越海洋的貿易與文化流動，成為人類不朽的記憶；正如今日矽晶經精密製程成為晶片，兩者皆源於相同的物質基礎，只是承載了不同時代的人類智慧。

Past is a Foreign Land explores how material culture preserves human memory across time while responding to the central theme of Between Carbon and Silicon. The exhibition presents seventeenth-century Zhangzhou and eighteenth-century Dehua ceramics, both produced in Fujian, China, as witnesses to Taiwan's history of migration and maritime exchange.


Ceramics represent one of the oldest media between carbon and silicon. Fired with carbon-based fuel and formed from silica-rich minerals—including quartz, feldspar, and Kaolin—they are transformed through intense heat before being shaped by the hands of the potter. These vessels carried trade, ideas, beliefs, and cultural exchange across the seas, becoming the enduring records of human civilization. In much the same way that refined silicon today undergoes highly precise fabrication to become semiconductor chips, both ceramics and microchips originate from the same material foundation yet embody the knowledge and technological achievements of different eras.


Displayed alongside these historical ceramics are five contemporary tablet-woven bands by Professor Yushan Tsai. Created by using tablet weaving, an ancient textile technique documented archaeologically across Central Asia, Europe, Egypt, and China, these works demonstrate how intricate patterns can be produced using only perforated cards and threads.


After decades of research on the textiles of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples, Professor Tsai turned her attention to contemporary tablet weaving following her retirement. Her recent works depict Taiwan's native birds, the Tung Blossom Festival, the World Baseball Classic, a Greek violinist friend, and plants from her own garden. Rooted in lived experience, these subjects celebrate the creativity of carbon-based life—people, animals, and plants—and its enduring capacity to generate culture.
By bringing together human craftsmanship and AI generation, historical ceramics and contemporary textile art, Past is a Foreign Land invites visitors to consider that civilization does not belong solely to the past. Rather, it continues to be preserved, translated, and regenerated between carbon and silicon.
